c: Roman province northwest of Macedonia. During the height of the Roman Empire (c.

117), when it included Dalmatia, Illyricum was bounded by the Adriatic Sea on the west and by the provinces of Pannonia on the north, Upper Moesia on the east, and Macedonia on the south. Today Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, and Yugoslavia occupy that territory.
, the people of Illyricum warred with the Macedonians, until the Macedonian ruler Philip II defeated them in 359
, their acts of piracy against Greek and Roman ships led to a war with Rome that continued on and off for 60 years (229–168
). After a series of revolts and sporadic Roman rule, Illyricum was officially made part of the empire in 11
and renamed Dalmatia. It took another 20 years for the people to be fully integrated into Roman culture.

the Roman historian Polybius stated that “the Illyrians were not the enemies of this people or that, but were the common enemies of all.” Later Strabo, a first-century Greek geographer, was still describing the people of Illyricum as savage and rapacious.

). Although Acts does not document a ministry in that region, Paul may have visited Illyricum during his visit to Macedonia and Achaia just before returning to Jerusalem (
). Paul expressed a desire to continue his ministry in Spain, a totally Latin environment (
); in Illyricum he would have had his first experience in a culture that was more Latin than Greek.
